title: Anyone else have a game idea that could take 2–3 years or more to finish?
author: dnr424
selftext:
Just wondering how many of you have a game idea or story you're really excited about, but know it'll take at least 2–3 years, maybe even longer, to actually bring it to life, even with the help of AI.

I'm in the same boat. I have a story I really want to turn into a game, but the scope is pretty ambitious. Ideally, I'd love to make it in full 3D, but realistically, that would be incredibly difficult to pull off as a solo developer. So I'm leaning towards 2.5D as a more manageable approach.

It's a strange feeling having a clear vision of what you want to create, but knowing how much time and effort it'll take to get there.

Anyone else in a similar situation? Have you had to compromise on your original vision to make your game achievable?

comments.author: GornoUmaethiVrurzu
comments.body: I'm doing full 3D. Turns out that's easier than 2.5D pixel art. Because assets get reused much easier. Like I'd have to draw a new image for every single attack, movement, etc on any characters, doubled if they're not symmetrical. Instead I spent a few hours modeling and animating one character and now it doesn't matter what I want, it always works. I can change looks and poses and animations and it all just works. Pixel art is also really hard to make look good. Both by human and AI. The AI does the coding, I do the modeling and textures and throw them into a level in blender, then export it to my engine. Much faster than pixel art tbh. Worth considering.

comments.author: FragmentedHeap
comments.body:
My dream game is a voxel engine, but instead of fixed cubes, they're ratios, with physics.  The idea is you dig a square hole in the ground.  But the water and mud from the surrounding blocks start seeping out and filling the hole you just dug, ratios are reduced from surrounding material as this happens. 

It rains and this is actually absorbed by the ground and changes the grounds water content and water table. 

You can take a big pond and then it rains and it fills up with water. 

Start building a big hole and digging a mine, but it quickly will collapse on you if you don't support it. 

Set off a giant explosion and all the math happens to understand what's going to happen to everything and then animates and explodes quickly without any lag. 

It's an incredibly complicated engine and it has a lot of math. 

And I don't think I could build it without AI. 

That's kind of my attitude I take with artificial intelligence. 

I want to push it and build things that wouldn't be possible without it. 

Not one shot stuff that's easy. 

Minecraft + garrysmod + factorio + satisfactory basically, on steroids

Dive in water where as you go down, pressure increases and you die, so you have to engineer a sub. 

I want to make it so you can build and engineer things in the game. 

Like designing an engine, and then putting it in a plane.

I want to do circuit designers too by having a real erd system where you design and simulate real circuits, where people learning to play the game actually learn basic electrical engineering skills.

replies.author: Mother-Hedgehog-5628
replies.body:
To ""I'm not trying to get millions of people to play my game..." The median lifetime gross revenue for all games released on Steam is roughly 200 to $3500 and "breakout" indy success targets are normally about 15k to 50k sales.

Even assuming you did hit the insane lottery of 100k units

**Steam’s Cut (30%):** Valve immediately takes **$449,700**, leaving $1,049,300.

**Regional Pricing and Sales:** Games are rarely sold at a flat $14.99 everywhere. Because of Steam’s regional pricing (e.g., cheaper in Brazil, Turkey, or Southeast Asia) and frequent seasonal discounts, the *average* actual price paid per copy is usually 20% to 30% lower than the base USD price. This drops the gross closer to **$1,100,000**, leaving about **$770,000** after Steam's cut.

**Refunds and Chargebacks:** Usually accounts for another 5% to 8% off the top.

**Taxes:** Depending on where the developer lives, corporate taxes and personal income tax on a massive lump sum will swallow another 25% to 40%.

After all that your probably in the $600,000 range, and again - thats assuming that insane number of 100k sales which is probably about 1% of indy games on steam.

Not to mention stuff like if your using unreal, then you start to have a royalty and licensing fee...

Yup, I’m living it right now lol.   
Started off with the idea of making a simple mobile game, started writing the story, used Ai to help me keep track of all the shit I was coming up with, then to tie all the loose ends up, sort it out chronologically and make it make sense, whilst in the mean time I’m inventing more and more shit. 

Now we have a story that would make George R.R and Tolkien hand their heads in shame, 3 games, 2 movies and a theatre production on broadway!!! 

THEN at that point I drop the bombshell of my mighty PC specs to said Ai. 

After it picked itself up off the floor laughing, told me I was a broke bitch with delusions of grandeur, helped me condense it down, take bits out, alter it till it’s now in an achievable state. Anything cut out has been kept in an ideas folder on my PC for when I eventually get some upgrades (cries in i5 and 750Ti), games progressing, of sorts and I’ve actually been able to keep some semblance of what I wanted in the first place. 

To Add I am a complete talentless old man who’s had a dream since he touched his first game to make his own. I’m using ai to help me make that dream come alive, finally!! 

And the best thing, is I’m making it FOR ME. If I ever finish it and decide to throw it out there, if people enjoy it, cool. If not, well it wasn’t for them ¯\\\_(ツ)\_/¯

comments.author: IAmFireAndFireIsMe
comments.body:
I’ve got four games that I’ve written the scripts for. 

One of them I truly believe is my masterpiece. I know, a-typical penis for thinking so but I adore this script. 

It’s short, a walking fpv game where you just need to get home. The story is scary and it does not let up. 

Now I had spent a year learning and trying to get this thing moving because I was never going to get hired at a studio and was never going to get funding to hire people to help me. 

What I can do is code, and I’ve been working with AI for about 10 years and while I mostly had it working on trying to understand fear the last year has changed the game for me. 

What Opus has managed to do in three months compared to my year is unbelievable. The game is mostly built, it hasn’t touched my story, it’s as tense as I imagined it would be and now I’m walking the world making sure things make sense to a player. 

I’m another three to six months away from launching it but I can’t believe how much is possible now to a single person. And if people are going to write compelling stories that wouldn’t get funding and they can just develop it all themselves, who cares if it’s made with AI? 

99% of the population don’t care. Tell them something amazing, don’t just slop away some crap that means nothing. 

Everyone can write something, don’t let your lack of knowledge be your blocker, just write stuff, people watch and just imagine what’s going on with other people, write about what scares you, excites you, what life you would have loved to have lived either today or 200 years ago. Anything. We’re at a time where your imagination can be played and experienced by others. 

Thanks for coming to my Ted Talk…

comments.author: Zaflis
comments.body:
\- Game based on wuxia novels, where character level isn't just going linearly from 1 to 100 or something but advances in phases and requirements for each large progress steps etc. They often include extremely large universes, even different dimensions of planets etc. Building portals, towns, civilizations etc. One could journey as a solo adventurer or build big. Death would result in resurrection somewhere with many of the previously learned things still available, almost like NewGame+ or perk points. One could always go and find previously obtained goods if you can find the location.

\- Similar or added to above game perhaps, RTS game with logistics systems that work on timing. Kind of reminds of Factorio too but systematically very different. Factorio doesn't support a game with a million planets that contain a megabase. This game's only bottleneck is available space on SSD since it doesn't even need to be contained in RAM. Because everything is caulculable from the timing, there is no need to calculate individual products moving through lines, and yes this game can have conveyor belts or some logistics drones/workers. They would move in a systematic way where duration of each round is always known and never changing. It is quite complicated to actually put it all together and some problems may occur when you change something in the middle of a long chain of production. It should still be possible even if it causes a little lagspike there.

Starships are an obvious feature in both games. Of which i've always been fascinated by Starcraft cutscenes of watching a protoss carrier entering a planet atmosphere looking from below.
